\section[\ar{آسف} / \ar{آسفة}]{\ar{آسف} / \ar{آسفة} (āsif / āsifa) — sorry}

\label{lesson:AR-C07-asif}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You already know \textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}}, "please." Arabic's word for "sorry" teaches a new lesson entirely: it isn't a fixed word at all — \textbf{it changes with the speaker.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{آسف}} (\emph{āsif}, said by a man) and \textbf{\ar{آسفة}} (\emph{āsifa}, said by a woman) both mean "\textbf{sorry}." They come from the verb \textbf{\ar{أَسِفَ}} (\emph{asifa}), "to grieve, to be filled with regret" — so saying \emph{āsif} is describing yourself as \emph{grieved / regretful}, the way you'd say "I am tired" or "I am happy."

That's the key: \textbf{\ar{آسف} is an adjective}, and Arabic adjectives \textbf{agree with the gender of the person they describe}. A man says \textbf{\ar{آسف}}; a woman says \textbf{\ar{آسفة}} — the extra \textbf{\ar{ة}} (\emph{tāʾ marbūṭa}) is the everyday feminine ending you'll meet across Arabic adjectives. English "sorry" never changes no matter who says it; Arabic "sorry" always tells you the speaker's gender in the same breath.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
For a quick, \textbf{ungendered} "excuse me / pardon" — squeezing past someone, interrupting, a light apology — Arabic reaches for \textbf{\ar{معذرة}} (\emph{maʿdhira}), from the root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ذ}-\ar{ر}} ("to excuse"), the same root as \textbf{\ar{عذر}} (\emph{ʿudhr}, "an excuse") and the verb \textbf{\ar{يعتذر}} (\emph{yaʿtadhiru}, "to apologize"). Unlike \emph{āsif/āsifa}, \textbf{\ar{معذرة} doesn't change with gender} — it's a noun, not an adjective, so anyone says the same word.

Use \textbf{\ar{آسف}/\ar{آسفة}} when you mean a real, felt "I'm sorry" (and remember to match your own gender); reach for \textbf{\ar{معذرة}} for the light, everyday "pardon me."
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: a man says — "āsif"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: a woman says — "āsifa"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the ungendered one — "maʿdhira" = excuse me / pardon{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What's unusual about \textbf{\ar{آسف} / \ar{آسفة}} compared to English "sorry"? (\textbf{It's a gendered adjective} — \emph{āsif} for a man, \emph{āsifa} for a woman — where English never changes.) What root gives \emph{āsif}, and what does it mean? (\textbf{\ar{أسف} asafa}, "to grieve, regret.") What's the ungendered word for a quick "excuse me," and what root is it from? (\textbf{\ar{معذرة} maʿdhira}, from \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ذ}-\ar{ر}} "to excuse.")
\end{tcolorbox}
